difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (block-count arithmetic for an unspanned heap file with a block header) followed by the expected cost of a sequential scan for two query types and a 50:50 mix; routine computation, about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Blocking factor and block count of an unspanned heap file, then expected block accesses for a successful sequential search and a full scan under a mixed workload
stem:
A hospital laboratory stores $36{,}000$ fixed-length test-result records of $150$ bytes each in a **heap (unordered) file**. The disk block size is $4096$ bytes and every block begins with a $96$-byte header; the rest of the block holds whole records only (the organisation is **unspanned**). Blocks are filled completely in sequence, so only the last block can be partly empty.

The workload consists of two kinds of queries, each making up half of all queries:

- *Key lookup:* fetch the record with a given key value that is known to be in the file. Blocks are read one after another starting from the first block, and the search stops as soon as the record is found. The record is equally likely to lie in any block of the file.
- *Non-key selection:* retrieve every record having a given value of a non-key attribute, which requires reading every block of the file.

The expected number of block accesses per query, averaged over this workload, is ________ (Answer in integer).

solution.quick:
Usable space per block is $4096-96=4000$ bytes, so $\lfloor 4000/150\rfloor = 26$ records fit and the file needs $b=\lceil 36000/26\rceil = 1385$ blocks.
A successful key lookup averages $(b+1)/2 = 693$ accesses and a non-key selection reads all $b = 1385$ blocks.
Averaging the two query types equally gives $\tfrac12(693)+\tfrac12(1385) = 1039$.

steps.title: Records per block (unspanned)
steps.body:
Usable bytes per block $= 4096 - 96 = 4000$. Because records may not span blocks, the blocking factor is

$$bf = \left\lfloor \frac{4000}{150} \right\rfloor = \lfloor 26.67 \rfloor = 26.$$

(Each block wastes $4000 - 26\cdot 150 = 100$ bytes.)

steps.title: Number of blocks in the file
steps.body:
$$b = \left\lceil \frac{36000}{26} \right\rceil = \lceil 1384.6\ldots \rceil = 1385.$$

Check: $26 \times 1384 = 35984$ records fill $1384$ blocks, so the remaining $16$ records need one more, partly filled, block.

steps.title: Expected cost of each query type
steps.body:
*Key lookup.* If the record lies in block $i$, the scan reads $i$ blocks. With $i$ equally likely over $1,\dots,b$:

$$E = \frac{1+2+\cdots+b}{b} = \frac{b+1}{2} = \frac{1386}{2} = 693.$$

*Non-key selection.* Every block must be read, so the cost is $b = 1385$.

solution.shortcut: For a 50:50 mix the average is $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{b+1}{2}+\tfrac12\cdot b = \dfrac{3b+1}{4}$. With $b = 1385$ this is $\dfrac{4156}{4} = 1039$.
solution.commonTrap: Ignoring the $96$-byte header (taking $\lfloor 4096/150\rfloor = 27$ records per block gives $b = 1334$ and $1000.75$), or rounding the block count down instead of up ($b = 1384$ gives $1038.25$), or using $b/2$ instead of $(b+1)/2$ for the successful lookup ($1038.75$).

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — combines independence, the sum of two binomials and conditioning, and needs the non-routine insight that the conditional law is hypergeometric (the success probability cancels), with a tempting binomial-with-$5/12$ trap; about 4 minutes.
concept: Conditional distribution of one binomial count given the total of two independent binomial counts with a common success probability (hypergeometric)
stem:
Two independent test benches inspect chips from the same production line. Bench 1 tests $5$ chips and bench 2 tests $7$ chips. Every chip tested, on either bench, fails independently with the same probability $0.3$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the numbers of failing chips on bench 1 and bench 2 respectively.

It is known that exactly $4$ chips failed in total, that is, $X + Y = 4$.

The probability that at least $2$ of these $4$ failures occurred on bench 1 is ________ (rounded off to three decimal places).

solution.quick:
Given $X+Y=4$, the $4$ failures are a random sample of $4$ of the $12$ tested chips, so $X$ is hypergeometric: $P(X=j\mid X+Y=4)=\dfrac{\binom{5}{j}\binom{7}{4-j}}{\binom{12}{4}}$, with the failure probability $0.3$ cancelling out.
Hence $P(X\ge 2\mid X+Y=4)=\dfrac{210+70+5}{495}=\dfrac{19}{33}\approx 0.576$.

steps.title: Set up the model
steps.body: $X\sim\text{Binomial}(5,\,p)$ and $Y\sim\text{Binomial}(7,\,p)$ are independent with $p=0.3$, so $X+Y\sim\text{Binomial}(12,\,p)$. We need $P(X\ge 2 \mid X+Y=4)$.

steps.title: Conditional pmf of $X$ given the total
steps.body:
For $j=0,\dots,4$,

$$P(X=j\mid X+Y=4)=\frac{P(X=j)\,P(Y=4-j)}{P(X+Y=4)}=\frac{\binom{5}{j}\binom{7}{4-j}\,p^{4}q^{8}}{\binom{12}{4}\,p^{4}q^{8}}=\frac{\binom{5}{j}\binom{7}{4-j}}{\binom{12}{4}},\qquad q=1-p.$$

The factor $p^4q^8$ is the same in numerator and denominator, so $p=0.3$ plays no role: the $4$ failures behave like $4$ chips drawn without replacement from the $12$ tested chips, $5$ of which are on bench 1.

solution.shortcut: Whenever independent binomials share the same $p$, conditioning on their total gives a hypergeometric law, so no powers of $p$ or $q$ need to be computed at all.
solution.commonTrap: Treating each of the $4$ failures as independently falling on bench 1 with probability $5/12$ (a binomial with replacement) gives $0.553$, and ignoring the condition and using $P(X\ge 2)$ for $X\sim\text{Binomial}(5,0.3)$ gives $0.472$. Neither matches the without-replacement structure of the conditional law.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (translating a nested-quantifier statement) with four equivalent or look-alike formulas that must each be checked through De Morgan, quantifier-order and implication-guard reasoning; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Translating 'every faulty sensor has a non-faulty backup' into first-order logic and recognising equivalent forms and a quantifier-order error
stem:
Let the domain be all devices in a plant (a non-empty set). Define the predicates

- $\text{Sensor}(x)$: $x$ is a sensor,
- $\text{Faulty}(x)$: $x$ is faulty,
- $\text{Backup}(y, x)$: $y$ is a backup of $x$.

Which of the following first-order formulas correctly express the statement below?

> Every faulty sensor has a backup that is not faulty.

solution.quick:
The natural translation is $\forall x\,\big((\text{Sensor}(x)\wedge\text{Faulty}(x))\rightarrow\exists y\,(\text{Backup}(y,x)\wedge\neg\text{Faulty}(y))\big)$, which is the second formula.
The third is its De Morgan form and the fourth is equivalent because $\exists y$ can be moved across an implication whose antecedent does not mention $y$. The first swaps the quantifiers and demands one common non-faulty backup for all faulty sensors.

steps.title: Write the direct translation
steps.body:
'Every faulty sensor has ...' is a universal statement guarded by an implication: for every device $x$, **if** $x$ is a faulty sensor **then** some $y$ is a backup of $x$ and is not faulty.

$$\Phi \;=\; \forall x\,\big((\text{Sensor}(x)\wedge\text{Faulty}(x)) \rightarrow \exists y\,(\text{Backup}(y,x)\wedge\neg\text{Faulty}(y))\big).$$

This is the second formula.

steps.title: The third formula is the De Morgan form of $\Phi$
steps.body:
Write $P(x)=	ext{Sensor}(x)\wedge	ext{Faulty}(x)$. Then

$$
eg ig(P(x)\wedge orall y\,(	ext{Backup}(y,x)ightarrow	ext{Faulty}(y)) ig)\equiv 
eg P(x)\vee\exists y\,
eg(
eg	ext{Backup}(y,x)\vee	ext{Faulty}(y))\equiv P(x)ightarrow\exists y\,(	ext{Backup}(y,x)\wedge
eg	ext{Faulty}(y)).$$

It says that no faulty sensor has all of its backups faulty (a faulty sensor with no backup at all is also excluded, because then 'all backups are faulty' holds vacuously).

steps.title: The fourth formula is equivalent because $y$ is not free in the antecedent
steps.body: For a fixed $x$, $\exists y\,(P(x)\rightarrow Q(x,y))\equiv P(x)\rightarrow\exists y\,Q(x,y)$ in a non-empty domain: if $P(x)$ is false, any $y$ makes the implication true; if $P(x)$ is true, we need some $y$ with $Q(x,y)$. With $Q(x,y)=\text{Backup}(y,x)\wedge\neg\text{Faulty}(y)$ this is exactly $\Phi$.

steps.title: The first formula is strictly stronger
steps.body: $\exists y\,\forall x\,(\dots)$ asserts a **single** non-faulty device $y$ that is a backup of every faulty sensor. Counter-model: devices $s_1, s_2$ (faulty sensors), $b_1, b_2$ (non-faulty), with $b_1$ the only backup of $s_1$ and $b_2$ the only backup of $s_2$. Then $\Phi$ holds, but no single $y$ works for both $s_1$ and $s_2$, so the first formula is false. Hence it does not express the statement.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Quantifier order is swapped: it needs one non-faulty device that backs up every faulty sensor. In the model with faulty sensors $s_1,s_2$ and distinct non-faulty backups $b_1,b_2$, the statement is true but this formula is false.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. This is the direct translation: every device that is a faulty sensor has some backup that is not faulty.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. It forbids a faulty sensor all of whose backups are faulty (or that has none); by De Morgan this is $\neg(\text{Sensor}\wedge\text{Faulty})\vee\exists y\,(\text{Backup}(y,x)\wedge\neg\text{Faulty}(y))$, the same as the second formula.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. Because the antecedent does not contain $y$, $\exists y\,(P\rightarrow Q(y))\equiv P\rightarrow\exists y\,Q(y)$ over a non-empty domain, so this equals the second formula.

solution.shortcut: Test each option on the tiny model $\{s_1,s_2,b_1,b_2\}$ with different backups for the two faulty sensors: only the formula that fixes one $y$ for all $x$ fails. The other three keep $y$ inside the scope of each $x$, so they agree with the statement.
solution.commonTrap: Rejecting the fourth formula because an implication sits directly under $\exists y$ (the rule $\exists y\,(P\rightarrow Q)$ with $y$ absent from $P$ is safe), and accepting the first formula because $\exists y\,\forall x$ and $\forall x\,\exists y$ look interchangeable.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept ($k$-means with Lloyd's iterations) that needs three assignment steps on six two-dimensional points and a sum of squared distances at convergence; routine but lengthy arithmetic, about 3 minutes.
concept: Running Lloyd's $k$-means to convergence and computing the final within-cluster sum of squared distances
stem:
Six soil samples are described by a nitrogen index $x$ and a moisture index $y$.

| Sample | $S_1$ | $S_2$ | $S_3$ | $S_4$ | $S_5$ | $S_6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $(x, y)$ | $(0, 7)$ | $(4, 1)$ | $(4, 7)$ | $(6, 1)$ | $(6, 5)$ | $(6, 7)$ |

The samples are clustered by Lloyd's $k$-means algorithm with $k = 2$ and Euclidean distance. The initial centroids are the points of $S_3$ and $S_6$. In each iteration every sample is first assigned to its nearest centroid, and then each centroid is replaced by the mean of the samples assigned to it. The algorithm stops when an assignment step leaves every centroid unchanged.

At termination, the within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances from each sample to the centroid of its cluster is

solution.quick:
Iteration 1 gives clusters $\{S_1,S_2,S_3\}$ and $\{S_4,S_5,S_6\}$; iteration 2 moves $S_2$ to the second cluster, giving $\{S_1,S_3\}$ with centroid $(2,7)$ and $\{S_2,S_4,S_5,S_6\}$ with centroid $(5.5,3.5)$; iteration 3 changes nothing.
The final sum of squared distances is $8 + 30 = 38$.

steps.title: Iteration 2: reassign and update
steps.body:
Only $S_2$ is borderline: $d_1^2=\left(\tfrac43\right)^2+16=\tfrac{160}{9}\approx 17.8$ and $d_2^2=2^2+\left(\tfrac{10}{3}\right)^2=\tfrac{136}{9}\approx 15.1$, so $S_2$ moves to cluster 2. $S_1$ and $S_3$ stay in cluster 1 (for $S_3$: $\approx 5.8$ against $\approx 11.1$), and $S_4,S_5,S_6$ stay in cluster 2.

Clusters: $\{S_1,S_3\}$ and $\{S_2,S_4,S_5,S_6\}$. New centroids: $c_1=(2,7)$ and $c_2=\left(\tfrac{4+6+6+6}{4},\tfrac{1+1+5+7}{4}\right)=(5.5,\,3.5)$.

steps.title: Iteration 3: confirm convergence
steps.body: With $c_1=(2,7)$ and $c_2=(5.5,3.5)$: $S_2$ has $d_1^2=40$, $d_2^2=8.5$ (cluster 2); $S_3$ has $d_1^2=4$, $d_2^2=14.5$ (cluster 1); $S_1$ is clearly closer to $c_1$; $S_4,S_5,S_6$ are clearly closer to $c_2$. No assignment changes, so the centroids stay put and the algorithm stops.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $14.58$ is the sum of plain (unsquared) Euclidean distances at the final centroids, $4+10.58$. The $k$-means objective uses squared distances.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. At convergence the clusters are $\{S_1,S_3\}$ and $\{S_2,S_4,S_5,S_6\}$ with centroids $(2,7)$ and $(5.5,3.5)$, giving $8+30=38$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $50.67 = 152/3$ is the sum of squared distances for the second assignment measured from the centroids of iteration 1, before they are recomputed from the new clusters.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $53.33 = 160/3$ is the objective after only one assign-and-update step, with $S_2$ still in the first cluster. The algorithm has not yet converged at that point.

solution.commonTrap: Stopping after the first update (clusters $\{S_1,S_2,S_3\}$, $\{S_4,S_5,S_6\}$), which gives $53.33$, or forgetting to square the distances. The assignment of $S_2$ flips in the second iteration because its nearest centroid changes once the centroids move.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (eigenvalues from trace, power-trace and a singularity condition) needing a short system for the remaining eigenvalues and a product over shifted eigenvalues; about 1.5 to 2 minutes.
concept: Recovering all eigenvalues from trace(A), trace(A^2) and one known eigenvalue, then evaluating det(A + I) as a product over eigenvalues
stem:
Let $A$ be a real $3 \times 3$ matrix and let $I$ be the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix. It is given that

$$\operatorname{trace}(A) = 9,\qquad \operatorname{trace}(A^{2}) = 29,\qquad \det(A - 2I) = 0.$$

The value of $\det(A + I)$ is

solution.quick:
$\det(A-2I)=0$ means $2$ is an eigenvalue. The other two satisfy $\lambda_2+\lambda_3=7$ and $\lambda_2^2+\lambda_3^2=25$, so $\lambda_2\lambda_3=12$ and $\{\lambda_2,\lambda_3\}=\{3,4\}$.
Therefore $\det(A+I)=(2+1)(3+1)(4+1)=60$.

steps.title: Use the eigenvalue facts
steps.body: Counting algebraic multiplicity, $\operatorname{trace}(A)=\sum\lambda_i$, $\operatorname{trace}(A^2)=\sum\lambda_i^2$ and $\det(A+I)=\prod(\lambda_i+1)$. Since $\det(A-2I)=0$, one eigenvalue is $\lambda_1=2$.

steps.title: Eliminate the known eigenvalue
steps.body: $$\lambda_2+\lambda_3 = 9-2 = 7,\qquad \lambda_2^2+\lambda_3^2 = 29-4 = 25.$$

steps.title: Find the other two eigenvalues
steps.body:
$$\lambda_2\lambda_3=\frac{(\lambda_2+\lambda_3)^2-(\lambda_2^2+\lambda_3^2)}{2}=\frac{49-25}{2}=12.$$

So $\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ are the roots of $x^2-7x+12=(x-3)(x-4)$, that is $3$ and $4$. The eigenvalues of $A$ are $2,3,4$ (check: sum $9$, sum of squares $4+9+16=29$).

steps.title: Evaluate the determinant
steps.body:
The eigenvalues of $A+I$ are $\lambda_i+1=3,4,5$, so

$$\det(A+I)=3\cdot 4\cdot 5=60.$$

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $20=4\cdot5$ drops the factor $2+1=3$ contributed by the known eigenvalue $2$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $25=\det(A)+1$ uses $\det A=24$ and wrongly assumes $\det(A+I)=\det(A)+\det(I)$; determinants are not additive.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. The eigenvalues are $2,3,4$, so $\det(A+I)=3\cdot4\cdot5=60$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $96$ comes from forgetting the division by $2$ when finding $\lambda_2\lambda_3$ (using $24$ instead of $12$): $3\,(24+7+1)=96$.

solution.shortcut: From $e_1=9$ and $e_2=\dfrac{9^2-29}{2}=26$, the characteristic polynomial is $p(x)=x^3-9x^2+26x-e_3$. Since $p(2)=0$, $8-36+52-e_3=0$ gives $e_3=24$, so $p(x)=(x-2)(x-3)(x-4)$ and $\det(A+I)=-p(-1)=60$.
solution.commonTrap: Forgetting that $\operatorname{trace}(A^2)=\sum\lambda_i^2$ gives $\lambda_2\lambda_3$ only after halving $(\sum\lambda)^2-\sum\lambda^2$; omitting the $/2$ leads to the tempting value $96$. Another trap is to treat $\det(A+I)$ as $\det(A)+1$.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — several steps (marginal over a triangular support, conditional density, two conditional moments and the variance) with a likely trap of treating the conditional density as flat or reporting a raw moment; about 4.5 minutes.
concept: Conditional variance of X given Y = y from a joint pdf on a triangular support
stem:
The joint probability density function of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$, the normalised capacity of a storage buffer and its normalised occupancy, is

$$
f_{X,Y}(x, y) = \begin{cases} 3x, & 0 < y < x < 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
$$

The conditional variance $\operatorname{Var}\!\left(X \mid Y = \tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is

solution.quick:
$f_Y(y)=\tfrac32(1-y^2)$, so $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid \tfrac12)=\tfrac{8x}{3}$ on $\tfrac12<x<1$.
Then $E[X\mid Y=\tfrac12]=\tfrac79$ and $E[X^2\mid Y=\tfrac12]=\tfrac58$, so the variance is $\tfrac58-\tfrac{49}{81}=\tfrac{13}{648}$.

steps.title: Marginal density of $Y$
steps.body:
For fixed $y$, $x$ runs from $y$ to $1$:

$$f_Y(y)=\int_{y}^{1}3x\,dx=\frac{3}{2}\,(1-y^{2}),\qquad 0<y<1.$$

(The joint density is already normalised: $\int_0^1\!\int_0^x 3x\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1 3x^2\,dx=1$.)

steps.title: Conditional density of $X$ given $Y=y$
steps.body:
$$f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{3x}{\tfrac32(1-y^2)}=\frac{2x}{1-y^{2}},\qquad y<x<1.$$

At $y=\tfrac12$: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid\tfrac12)=\dfrac{2x}{3/4}=\dfrac{8x}{3}$ for $\tfrac12<x<1$. Check: $\int_{1/2}^{1}\tfrac{8x}{3}\,dx=\tfrac43\left(1-\tfrac14\right)=1$.

steps.title: Conditional moments
steps.body:
$$E\!\left[X\mid Y=\tfrac12\right]=\int_{1/2}^{1}x\cdot\frac{8x}{3}\,dx=\frac{8}{9}\left(1-\frac18\right)=\frac79,$$

$$E\!\left[X^{2}\mid Y=\tfrac12\right]=\int_{1/2}^{1}x^{2}\cdot\frac{8x}{3}\,dx=\frac{2}{3}\left(1-\frac1{16}\right)=\frac58.$$

steps.title: Variance
steps.body: $$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(X\mid Y=\tfrac12\right)=\frac58-\left(\frac79\right)^{2}=\frac58-\frac{49}{81}=\frac{405-392}{648}=\frac{13}{648}\approx 0.0201.$$

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $E[X^2\mid Y=\tfrac12]-\left(E[X\mid Y=\tfrac12]\right)^2=\tfrac58-\tfrac{49}{81}=\tfrac{13}{648}$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\tfrac1{48}$ is the variance of a uniform distribution on $\left(\tfrac12,1\right)$, i.e. $\tfrac{(1/2)^2}{12}$. The conditional density $\tfrac{8x}{3}$ is not flat; it favours larger $x$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\tfrac{3}{80}$ is the unconditional $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ for $f_X(x)=3x^2$ (since $E[X]=\tfrac34$, $E[X^2]=\tfrac35$), which ignores the condition $Y=\tfrac12$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\tfrac58$ is the conditional second moment $E[X^2\mid Y=\tfrac12]$; the squared conditional mean has not been subtracted.

solution.commonTrap: Assuming that because the density $3x$ has no $y$ in it, $X$ is simply uniform on $(y,1)$ (giving $\tfrac1{48}$), or stopping at $E[X^2\mid Y=\tfrac12]=\tfrac58$ without subtracting the squared mean. The lower limit of the support, $x>y$, is what makes the conditional density $\tfrac{2x}{1-y^2}$.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — one concept (linear search) and a direct trace of four short searches on an eight-element list, counting comparisons; about 2 minutes.
concept: Tracing a backward linear search that returns the position and the number of comparisons, for successful and unsuccessful queries
stem:
Consider the following Python program.

```python
def scan_back(a, key):
    steps = 0
    i = len(a) - 1
    while i >= 0:
        steps += 1
        if a[i] == key:
            return i, steps
        i -= 1
    return -1, steps

data = [6, 2, 9, 2, 5, 6, 1, 8]
total = 0
misses = 0
for k in [2, 6, 7, 8]:
    pos, steps = scan_back(data, k)
    total += steps
    if pos == -1:
        misses += 1
print(total, misses)
```

The output of the program is

solution.quick:
`scan_back` examines the list from the right end and stops at the first match, so it finds the **last** occurrence. The numbers of comparisons are $5$ (key 2), $3$ (key 6), $8$ (key 7, not found) and $1$ (key 8).
So `total` $=5+3+8+1=17$ and `misses` $=1$; the program prints `17 1`.

steps.title: Understand the search
steps.body: The loop starts at index $7$ and moves left, adding one to `steps` for every element it compares with `key`. It returns as soon as `a[i] == key` (the last occurrence of the key) and reaches `return -1, steps` only after comparing all $8$ elements. The list holds $6, 2, 9, 2, 5, 6, 1, 8$ at indices $0$ to $7$.

steps.title: Accumulate the counters
steps.body: `total` $=5+3+8+1=17$. Only the query for key $7$ returns `pos == -1`, so `misses` $=1$. The program prints `17 1`.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: `14 1` counts the distance of the matching index from the right end (zero-based: $4+2+8+0$) instead of the number of comparisons, which is one more for each successful search.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: `19 1` is the total for a left-to-right scan ($2+1+8+8$), which would find the first occurrence of each key. This program scans from the right.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: `16 1` counts only $7$ comparisons for the unsuccessful search, as if index $0$ were never examined; the loop condition `i >= 0` does examine it, giving $8$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. The comparison counts are $5, 3, 8, 1$, which sum to $17$, and there is exactly one miss.

solution.commonTrap: Reading the loop as a forward search (it starts at `len(a) - 1` and goes left) or miscounting the unsuccessful search for key $7$, which must examine all $8$ elements, including index $0$.

def scan_back(a, key):
    steps = 0
    i = len(a) - 1
    while i >= 0:
        steps += 1
        if a[i] == key:
            return i, steps
        i -= 1
    return -1, steps
data = [6, 2, 9, 2, 5, 6, 1, 8]
total = 0
misses = 0
for k in [2, 6, 7, 8]:
    pos, steps = scan_back(data, k)
    total += steps
    if pos == -1:
        misses += 1
print(total, misses)

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (rank of a parametric matrix) whose four statements each need a separate check (rank, nullity, consistency and the rank of $A^\top A$); about 3.5 minutes.
concept: Rank, nullity and consistency of a matrix with a parameter that makes the rows dependent for one value, and the rank of A^T A
stem:
For a real parameter $k$, let

$$A(k)=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0&1\\2&4&1&3\\3&6&1&k\end{bmatrix}.$$

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The $4\times4$ matrix $A(k)^{\top}A(k)$ is invertible for every real $k\neq4$.

options.label: C
options.text: For $\mathbf b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\\5\end{bmatrix}$, the system $A(k)\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is consistent for every real $k$.

options.label: D
options.text: When $k=4$, the null space of $A(k)$ has dimension $2$.

solution.quick:
Row reduction gives the echelon form with rows $(1,2,0,1)$, $(0,0,1,1)$, $(0,0,0,k-4)$, so $\operatorname{rank}A(k)=3$ for $k\neq4$ and $2$ for $k=4$.
Hence the nullity at $k=4$ is $4-2=2$. The system with $\mathbf b=(1,3,5)^\top$ is inconsistent at $k=4$, and $A^\top A$ ($4\times4$ with rank $\le3$) is never invertible.

steps.title: Row-reduce $A(k)$
steps.body:
$R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1=(0,0,1,1)$ and $R_3\leftarrow R_3-3R_1=(0,0,1,k-3)$. Then $R_3\leftarrow R_3-R_2=(0,0,0,k-4)$. The echelon form is

$$\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0&1\\0&0&1&1\\0&0&0&k-4\end{bmatrix}.$$

steps.title: Rank and nullity
steps.body: For $k\neq4$ there are three pivots (columns $1,3,4$), so $\operatorname{rank}A(k)=3$. For $k=4$ the last row vanishes, so $\operatorname{rank}A(4)=2$ (indeed row $3$ = row $1$ + row $2$). By the rank-nullity theorem the null space of the $3\times4$ matrix has dimension $4-\operatorname{rank}$, which is $1$ for $k\neq4$ and $2$ for $k=4$.

steps.title: Consistency for $\mathbf b=(1,3,5)^\top$
steps.body: Apply the same row operations to $\mathbf b$: $b_2'=3-2\cdot1=1$, $b_3'=5-3\cdot1=2$, then $b_3''=2-1=1$. The last row of the augmented system reads $0\cdot x_1+0\cdot x_2+0\cdot x_3+(k-4)x_4=1$. For $k\neq4$ it is solvable, but for $k=4$ it becomes $0=1$, so the system is **inconsistent** at $k=4$. (Equivalently, at $k=4$ consistency needs $b_3=b_1+b_2$, and $5\neq 4$.)

steps.title: The matrix $A^\top A$
steps.body: $\operatorname{rank}(A^\top A)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\le3<4$ for every $k$, so the $4\times4$ matrix $A^\top A$ is singular for **every** real $k$, including $k\neq4$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\operatorname{rank}(A^\top A)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\le3$, but $A^\top A$ is $4\times4$, so $\det(A^\top A)=0$ for every $k$. Four columns in $\mathbb R^3$ can never be independent.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. The three pivots appear exactly when the last entry $k-4$ is non-zero.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: At $k=4$ the rank drops to $2$ and the third row equals the sum of the first two, so $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is solvable only if $b_3=b_1+b_2$. For $\mathbf b=(1,3,5)^\top$ this fails ($5\neq4$), so the system is inconsistent at $k=4$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. At $k=4$ the rank is $2$, so the nullity is $4-2=2$.

solution.commonTrap: Assuming that full row rank (rank $3$ for $k\neq4$) makes the system solvable for every $k$, forgetting the exceptional value $k=4$ where a row dependency appears, and mixing up $A^\top A$ ($4\times4$, always singular here) with $AA^\top$ ($3\times3$, invertible exactly when $k\neq4$).

print('det of pivot-column block:', sp.factor(A[:,[0,2,3]].det()))

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (existence of an LU decomposition without row exchanges) needing elimination with a parameter and the distinction between a zero pivot and a singular matrix; about 3 minutes.
concept: Existence of an LU decomposition without row interchanges for a parametric matrix: zero pivot versus singularity
stem:
For a real parameter $t$, let

$$A(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&1\\3&t&4\\2&5&3\end{bmatrix}.$$

Say that $A(t)$ has an LU decomposition if $A(t)=LU$ for some lower triangular matrix $L$ with every diagonal entry equal to $1$ and some upper triangular matrix $U$ (no row interchanges are allowed).

Let $S$ be the set of real values of $t$ for which $A(t)$ is nonsingular but has **no** LU decomposition. Then

solution.quick:
Eliminating below the first pivot gives rows $(0,\,t-6,\,1)$ and $(0,\,1,\,1)$, so the second pivot is $t-6$ and $\det A(t)=t-7$.
For $t=6$ the second pivot is $0$ although the entry below it is $1\neq0$ and $\det A=-1\neq0$: no LU exists. For $t=7$ the matrix is singular, but only the last pivot vanishes, and an LU decomposition still exists. So $S=\{6\}$.

steps.title: Case $t\neq6$: the decomposition exists
steps.body: Then $l_{32}=\dfrac{1}{t-6}$ and $u_{33}=1-\dfrac{1}{t-6}=\dfrac{t-7}{t-6}$, so an LU decomposition exists. Multiplying the pivots, $\det A(t)=1\cdot(t-6)\cdot\dfrac{t-7}{t-6}=t-7$. In particular for $t=7$ the matrix is singular ($u_{33}=0$), but $L=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\3&1&0\\2&1&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $U=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}$ satisfy $LU=A(7)$.

steps.title: Case $t=6$: no decomposition although $A$ is nonsingular
steps.body: Here $\det A(6)=6-7=-1\neq0$. In $A=LU$ with unit $L$, $u_{22}=a_{22}-l_{21}u_{12}=6-3\cdot2=0$, while the $(3,2)$ entry requires $a_{32}=l_{31}u_{12}+l_{32}u_{22}$, i.e. $5=2\cdot2+l_{32}\cdot0=4$, a contradiction. Without a row exchange no LU decomposition exists.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The values of $t$ for which $A(t)$ is nonsingular ($t\neq7$) and has no LU decomposition (only $t=6$) intersect in $S=\{6\}$. The value $t=7$ is singular but does have an LU decomposition.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Not empty: at $t=6$ the matrix is nonsingular ($\det=-1$) yet the second pivot is zero while the entry below it is non-zero, so no LU decomposition exists without a row exchange.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $t=6$ makes the leading $2\times2$ minor $t-6$ vanish while $\det A(6)=-1\neq0$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $t=7$ is where $\det A(t)=t-7$ vanishes, so $A(7)$ is singular and not in $S$. Only the last pivot $u_{33}$ is zero, which does not prevent the factorisation $A(7)=LU$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: It wrongly includes $t=7$: $A(7)$ is singular, so it fails the 'nonsingular' requirement, and it still has an LU decomposition.

solution.shortcut: A nonsingular matrix has an LU decomposition without row exchanges exactly when its leading principal minors of orders $1,\dots,n-1$ are all non-zero. Here those minors are $1$ and $\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&t\end{bmatrix}=t-6$, so only $t=6$ fails, and $\det A(t)=t-7$ shows that $t=6$ is nonsingular.
solution.commonTrap: Confusing 'singular' with 'has no LU decomposition' and picking $\{7\}$ (the root of $\det A(t)$), or believing every nonsingular matrix has an LU decomposition without row exchanges and picking $\varnothing$.
